Archimedes. Born around 287 BCE and died 212 BCE, an ancient Greek mathematician, physicist, and engineer whose work in geometry, hydrostatics, and mechanics anticipated modern calculus by nearly two thousand years. Working in Syracuse in Sicily, he calculated areas and volumes using infinitesimal methods, the method of exhaustion, formulated the principle of buoyancy, and designed ingenious mechanical devices and weapons. His combination of rigorous proof, practical engineering, and mathematical daring made him perhaps the greatest mathematician of antiquity.

He calculated the area of a parabolic segment by exhaustion, approximating it with inscribed and circumscribed polygons, a precursor to integration. The method of exhaustion proved the area of a circle equals the product of its radius and half its circumference, that is, A equals pi times r squared, effectively computing pi. He approximated pi to remarkable precision, between three and one-seventh and three and ten seventy-firsts, a figure not significantly improved until the seventeenth century.

Archimedes' Principle states that a body immersed in fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced. This is foundational to hydrostatics. He calculated the volume of a sphere inscribed in a cylinder and proved it is two-thirds the volume of the cylinder. The Archimedean screw is a helical device for raising water that remains in use today. He may also have invented lever and pulley systems.

His work On Floating Bodies systematically studied stability and equilibrium of floating vessels. His war machines—catapults and mirrors for firing ships—defended Syracuse during its siege by Rome. He reportedly said, "Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth," illustrating the power of leverage.

Archimedes bridged the ancient and modern worlds. His method of exhaustion was rediscovered in the seventeenth century and directly influenced Leibniz and Newton's development of calculus. His infinitesimal reasoning was remarkably close to theirs, just expressed geometrically rather than algebraically. His Palimpsest, a medieval copy of his writings later erased and overwritten then rediscovered in the twentieth century, revealed methods he had kept private, proving he thought in ways far ahead of his era. He represents the apex of ancient mathematics. No Greek mathematician surpassed him, and even today his ingenuity astounds.
